title: What kosher means
hook: kosher means fit; some Jews keep the food laws fully, some partly, some not at all

segments.voice: Yesterday, tefillin, and how each community answers who wears them. Your line was customs differ, respect holds. Keep that line close this week, because today we open the Jewish food laws. Day one hundred forty-four.

You've probably used the word yourself. Is that kosher? Meaning: is that allowed, is that legit, is that okay? It's one of the Hebrew words that made it all the way into everyday English. Then there's the other place you've seen it: a little symbol on a box of crackers, or a sign in a deli window. Most people have a rough idea what it means. No pork. Something about meat and milk. A rabbi blessing the food, maybe? That last one isn't it. So what does kosher actually mean?
screen: `IS THAT KOSHER?` → `A SYMBOL ON THE CRACKERS.` → `WHAT DOES IT ACTUALLY MEAN?`

segments.voice: Kosher, or kasher in Hebrew, means fit, proper, right for its purpose. The word appears in the Bible in the book of Esther, when the queen asks the king for a favor, "and the thing seem right before the king." Right, fit: kasher. It isn't only about food. A Torah scroll can be kosher, fit for reading. A shofar can be kosher. A sukkah. The system of food laws is called kashrut, fitness. And no, food doesn't become kosher because a rabbi blesses it. It's kosher because of what it is and how it was prepared. Over the next few days, we'll go through it plainly: which animals the Torah permits, the separation of meat and milk, care for animals, and why people keep it. The basic outline is in the Torah, and rabbinic law built it out in detail. Kosher food also needs supervision, which is what those symbols on packages mean: an agency has checked the ingredients and the process. Now here's the part that surprises people. Not all Jews keep kosher, and those who do don't all keep it the same way. Some keep it fully, at home and away. Some keep a kosher home but eat more freely outside. Some avoid pork and shellfish and leave it there. Some don't keep it at all, and some keep an ethical version, focused on how food is raised. In America, surveys suggest a minority of Jews keep kosher at home. That's not a scorecard. It's a picture of a people making choices about something they take seriously. What almost everyone shares is the idea underneath: eating is never just eating. It's a choice, three times a day.
screen: `KASHER: FIT, PROPER, RIGHT.` · `NOT A BLESSING, A WAY OF PREPARING.` · `SOME FULLY, SOME PARTLY, SOME NOT.` · `EATING IS NEVER JUST EATING.` · then, large: `AND THE THING SEEM RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one food choice today. Start with the last thing you ate. Settle, and breathe. Where did it come from? Who made it? Did you choose it, or did it just happen? No judgment, just noticing. Then think of your next meal. Picture choosing it on purpose, for any reason that matters to you: health, kindness, tradition, gratitude. The bell holds the time.
Kosher. Fit, proper: food prepared according to Jewish law, and a word for anything right for its purpose.
Your line: eating is a choice. At one meal today, pause before the first bite and ask why you chose this food. Day one hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Jews who keep kosher eat only permitted foods, prepared and supervised according to Jewish law, often checking for a kosher symbol on packaged food. Observance ranges from full kashrut at home and away to partial or none.

original.note: Hebrew: fit, proper; English kosher comes through Yiddish.

trapdoor: what you thought: food a rabbi has blessed.
what it means: fit, proper; food chosen and prepared according to Jewish law, kept in many different ways.
what a scholar hears: kasher appears in Esther 8:5 and Ecclesiastes 11:6 and 10:10; the food laws are Torah outlines (Leviticus 11, Deuteronomy 14) expanded in the Talmud and codes.
